_about: Canonical Roman Urdu spellings for the tafsir translation, extracted by
frequency from assets/translations/ur-roman.json — the Roman Urdu Quran
translation the app already ships. Roman Urdu has no standard orthography,
so the only thing that makes the tafsir look native rather than generated
is agreeing with the translation printed directly above it on screen.
'use' is the spelling to write. 'avoid' lists variants that appear either
in the source itself (it is not internally consistent) or in ordinary
Roman Urdu, and that the checker flags.
Counts are occurrences in ur-roman.json at the time of extraction.

names._note: These deliberately differ from assets/tafsir/{en,fr,es,it}, which use Musa / Nuh / Dawud / Harun / Ayyub / Shu'ayb. Within a language, matching that language's own translation beats matching the other languages.

Jibreel._note: absent from the source; Jibreel matches its vowel habits (Ismaeel/Ibraheem family)

deen.gloss: religion — NOT 'din', which is the separate word for 'day' and appears 271 times in the source

terms._spelling_note: Below: ordinary (non-religious) words where the first tranche used a spelling the reference does not. Each pair was verified by counting both forms in ur-roman.json. These are the class of error a 90-term glossary misses, so they are pinned explicitly rather than left to a fuzzy matcher.

pahunchana.gloss: to convey, to reach — stem pahunch-, never pohanch-

tamaam.gloss: all — the reference uses both tamaam (53) and tamam (4); either is acceptable

bhadakna.gloss: to blaze — bharakna means to flare up in anger, a different word

yakta.gloss: unique, one — NOT akela, which means lonely and is doctrinally wrong of Allah

maabood.gloss: object of worship, deity — 'ilah' as a standalone noun appears 0 times in the reference

humsar.gloss: equal, peer — the reference's word at 112:4

shar.gloss: evil — preferred over buraai in surahs 113-114, where the reference uses it

rehzan.gloss: bandit — daaku is Hindi-register and absent from the reference

paida.gloss: to create — 'janam dena' is Hindi-register, said of mothers, and reads crudely of Allah

_note: WHO IS BEING ADDRESSED DECIDES THE VERB FORM. This is the single
easiest thing to get wrong across a whole edition, and it reads as
The Mukhtasar addresses the Prophet constantly ('Say, O Messenger',
'know that', 'you see'). In Urdu that must take the respectful aap
form, never the familiar tu form.

prophet.use: aap — respectful. keh dijiye, jaan lijiye, aap dekhein, aap ko, aap ke, tasbeeh kijiye, maangiye
prophet.avoid: tu — familiar. keh de, jaan le, tu dekhe, tujhe, tere, kar, maang
prophet.example: 'Aey Rasool, keh dijiye' — NOT 'Aey Rasool, keh de'

allah.use: tu — correct and reverent for Allah in Urdu, and what the app's own translation uses: 'Hum teri hi ibadat karte hain aur tujh hi se madad maangte hain' (1:5). Keep tu, tera, tujhe, tujh when the worshipper addresses Allah, as in 1:5-1:7.
allah.note: So tu-forms are not wrong in themselves — only wrong when aimed at the Prophet.

reader.use: aap or the neutral plural. The source's 'tum' (1514 occurrences) addresses people in general and is fine there.

continuation.note: A verse may continue an address begun in the previous verse without naming it again — 110:2 and 110:3 carry on from 110:1's 'Aey Rasool'. Check the preceding verse, not just the one in front of you.

register._note: The source's grammatical habits, for matching its voice.
register.vocative: Aey (437 occurrences). The reference's own vocatives for the Prophet are 'Aey Nabi' (186) and 'Aey Muhammad' (112); 'Aey Rasool' appears 0 times, though 'Rasool' as a noun appears 284 times. We use 'Aey Rasool ﷺ' because the Mukhtasar says 'O Messenger' rather than 'O Prophet' — a deliberate divergence, not an oversight.
register.khuda: appears 323 times alongside Allah; use Allah unless rendering 'god/deity' generically

_note: THE FAULT NO GLOSSARY OR CHECKER CATCHES. The glossary pins words;
nothing pins sentence construction, so construction defaults to the
English and the result is individually parseable but cumulatively
foreign — and reads as machine-made sitting next to Maududi's human
Translate the sentence, not the clause order. Every example below was
produced by translating word-for-word, and every one was caught by a
native speaker or an audit, not by a tool.

examples.why: 'alone in being a deity' word-for-word; 'akela' means lonely, which is doctrinally wrong of Allah
'acts out his jealousy' calqued; no Urdu speaker says 'hasad par amal karna'
one blows INTO knots, not onto them; the reference has the exact idiom at 113:4

examples.wrong: us ki zaat ke sath, us ki sifaat ke sath aur us ke kaamon ke sath
examples.right: us ki zaat, us ki sifaat aur us ke kaamon ke lihaz se

examples.wrong: jis mein tamam kaamil sifaat hain
examples.right: jo husn o kamaal ki tamam sifaat ka maalik hai
examples.why: locative calque; attributes are possessed, not contained

examples.right: us ke shar se jo nuqsan pahunchati hai
examples.why: collapses an English genitive chain into coordination, and mismatches singular with plural oblique

examples.wrong: woh khaas logon ko niyamat deta hai
examples.right: woh baaz bandon ko khusoosi tor par niyamat deta hai
examples.why: 'khaas log' means the elite in Urdu, importing a class distinction the English does not have
'aap log' is a fixed phrase ('you people'), so the reader parses it as a vocative before backtracking

examples.wrong: Yeh log kaise achhe saathi hain!
examples.why: 'yeh log' is flat-to-dismissive, and the referents are prophets and martyrs; the reference has the settled form at 4:69

no_calque.agreement: Check gender and number across clauses. A compound subject of mixed gender ('maal' m. + 'aulad' f.) must agree consistently: 'us ke kis kaam aa sakte hain', not 'aa sakti hai' followed by 'sakte hain' one clause later.
no_calque.tense: Keep the English's tense. 'who knew the truth and did not follow it' is past: 'jinhon ne haqq ko jaan kar bhi us ki pairwi na ki', not the present 'nahin karte'.
no_calque.fixed_phrases: Where the reference already has a liturgical or idiomatic phrase, use its wording verbatim rather than inventing one: 'ambiya, siddiqeen, shuhada aur saliheen' (4:69), 'girhon mein phoonkne walon' (113:4), 'koi uska humsar nahin' (112:4), 'woh Allah hai, Yakta' (112:1).

honorifics._note: Match assets/tafsir/{en,...}: one per name per verse, none where the surrounding text already supplies one, a collective form for a list of three or more.
